title: Entropic Necks, Dynamic Crossovers, and Fragility in Supercooled Liquids
abstract: The dramatic slowdown of dynamics in supercooled liquids is accompanied by a sequence of dynamical crossovers, most notably the transition from high-temperature collision-dominated transport to low-temperature activated structural relaxation. A particularly striking manifestation of this change is the crossover from Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling to the Adam--Gibbs relation. In this work we develop a theoretical framework based on a configuration-space extension of Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture and combine it with a Mori--Zwanzig memory-function formalism to address anomalies of supercooled liquids. The central idea is that structural relaxation is controlled by the narrowing of configurational pathways connecting metastable basins of the inherent-structure landscape. Starting from coupled slow variables describing intrabasin motion and neck fluctuations, we derive a reduced generalized Langevin description in which elimination of the neck coordinate generates a long-lived memory kernel and naturally leads to entropy-controlled activated dynamics. At high temperatures the neck is broad and readily accessible, yielding Rosenfeld-type transport governed primarily by local structural entropy. Upon cooling, progressive neck constriction produces an increasing entropy deficit, leading to Adam--Gibbs behavior and activated relaxation. Within this picture, fragility acquires a simple geometric interpretation: fragile liquids are characterized by a rapid collapse of the effective configurational neck with decreasing temperature, whereas strong liquids exhibit a much slower evolution of accessible pathways. The framework does not by itself compute the configurational entropy, mismatch penalty, or cooperative length from microscopic interactions; its aim is to provide a dynamical and geometrical interpretation.
summary: This work develops a unified theoretical framework by merging the entropic-neck picture with the Mori-Zwanzig formalism to explain glassy slowing down. It demonstrates that structural relaxation is governed by the entropy loss associated with passing through narrow configurational bottlenecks. This mechanism naturally explains the crossover from high-temperature local dynamics (Rosenfeld scaling) to low-temperature activated behavior (Adam-Gibbs relation).
main_problem: The work addresses the origin of the dramatic dynamical slowdown observed in supercooled liquids, specifically explaining the crossover between high-temperature local dynamics and low-temperature activated structural relaxation.
main_result: A unified theoretical framework is developed showing that structural relaxation is controlled by the narrowing of configurational pathways (entropic bottlenecks), naturally unifying Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling with the Adam-Gibbs relation.
method: The authors combine Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture with the Mori-Zwanzig memory-function formalism to derive an effective generalized Langevin equation for slow variables.
model_or_system: The system is supercooled liquids whose dynamics are mapped onto a configuration space featuring metastable basins separated by narrow, entropy-controlling 'necks.' The model uses coupled slow variables: progress (interbasin motion) and neck openness.
key_observables: Relaxation times ($	au(T)$), configurational entropy ($S_{conf}$), excess entropy ($S_{ex}$), and the effective memory kernel components.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), Configurational Entropy ($s_c(T)$), Neck Deficit ($\Delta\Sigma_{	ext{neck}}$), and the crossover temperature $T_{cross}$.
main_assumptions: The theory assumes that structural relaxation can be decomposed into dynamics governed by local structure (high T) and rare, cooperative passage through narrow entropic bottlenecks (low T). The derivation relies on linearizing the free-energy surface near these bottlenecks.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the entropic bottleneck picture, showing progress ($X$) between basins connected by a variable cross-section neck ($Q$), which dictates the effective potential and memory kernel.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the physical problem (slowdown) to introducing the theoretical tools (Mori-Zwanzig/Entropic Neck). It then derives the dynamics, showing how eliminating the fast neck coordinate generates a long-lived, entropy-controlled memory kernel that dictates the crossover between RS and AG regimes.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of projection operator techniques (Mori-Zwanzig) to derive non-Markovian memory kernels from geometric constraints (the bottleneck) provides a powerful template for understanding slow dynamics in complex many-body systems, applicable beyond simple liquids.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic representation of Zwanzig’s entropic bottleneck picture in configura- tion space. The coordinate X denotes progress between neighboring metastable basins, while Q denotes a schematic transverse neck coordinate that represents the instantaneous openness or configurational accessibility of the bottleneck. Wide regions correspond to basins and narrow but finite regions correspond to entropic necks. The local width A(X) measures the effective number of accessible configurations at a given X and defines an entropic potential F(X) = −kBT ln A(X). Thus constricted regions act as entropic bar- riers that reduce the probability of interbasin passage.
